core: working definition (CDC-attributed): standard precautions are the infection-prevention practices used for EVERY patient's care, regardless of diagnosis — the basic level of infection control precautions used as a minimum in the care of all patients
the every-patient idea: assume anyone's blood and body fluids may carry germs — standard precautions reduce transmission from both recognized and unrecognized sources, with an original example
components named: hand hygiene, gloves, gowns, masks (face protection), safe injection practices, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, environmental cleaning, linens — each with one line
PPE basics: gloves when contact with blood/body fluids likely, gown when splashes likely; gear chosen by risk assessment
safe injection practice: one needle, one syringe, only one time (CDC One & Only Campaign), attributed
respiratory hygiene: cover coughs and sneezes, masks for coughers, distance in waiting areas
honest framing: standard precautions are the default, not the exception — the reality check
supporting: CDC page lists hand hygiene, PPE, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, patient placement, equipment cleaning/disinfection, environmental cleaning, textiles/laundry, safe injection practices, sharps safety as elements

WHO aide-memoire (October 2007) lists 10 key elements: hand hygiene; gloves; facial protection; gown; prevention of needle-stick/sharp injuries; respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette; environmental cleaning; linens; waste disposal; patient care equipment
WHO PPE selection: clean non-sterile gloves, clean non-sterile fluid-resistant gown, mask and eye protection or face shield
CDC One & Only Campaign: safe injection practices are part of standard precautions; 'one needle, one syringe, only one time'

claims.claim: Standard precautions are the basic level of infection-control precautions to be used, as a minimum, in the care of all patients; they are meant to reduce the risk of transmission of bloodborne and other pathogens from both recognized and unrecognized sources.

The CDC states standard precautions are used for all patient care; they are based on a risk assessment and make use of common-sense practices and personal protective equipment that protect healthcare providers from infection and prevent the spread of infection from patient to patient.

The core elements of standard precautions include hand hygiene; gloves; gowns; masks and facial protection; safe injection practices; respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette; environmental cleaning; and careful handling of linens — a bundle each source lists with minor variation.

PPE is selected by risk assessment: clean non-sterile gloves when touching blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes or non-intact skin; a clean non-sterile fluid-resistant gown when splashes or sprays of blood or body fluids are likely; and a mask with eye protection or a face shield when splashes or sprays may reach the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Safe injection practice follows the rule of the CDC's One & Only Campaign: one needle, one syringe, only one time — a fresh, sterile needle and syringe for every injection; safe injection practices are part of standard precautions.

Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette are part of standard precautions: people with respiratory symptoms should cover their nose and mouth when coughing or sneezing (with a tissue or mask), perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions, and be kept at some distance from others in waiting areas.
Environmental cleaning under standard precautions means adequate procedures for routine cleaning and disinfection of environmental and other frequently touched surfaces.
Linens are handled, transported, and processed so that used linen does not cause skin or mucous membrane exposure, contaminate clothing, or transfer pathogens to other patients or the environment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact component list varies between sources
positions: WHO aide-memoire (2007) lists 10 elements including waste disposal and patient care equipment, with sharps-injury prevention as its own element

CDC's standard precautions page (2024) lists hand hygiene, PPE, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, patient placement, equipment cleaning, environmental cleaning, textiles/laundry, safe injection, and sharps safety
Some later summaries fold sharps safety and waste handling into 'safe injection practices' and 'environmental cleaning'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the eight components named in the assignment (hand hygiene, gloves, gowns, masks, safe injection, respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning, linens) — all present in both the CDC and WHO lists — and notes the lists vary slightly by source without going into full enumeration.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Standard precautions 'for everyone' versus 'based on risk assessment'
positions: The baseline applies to all patients regardless of diagnosis (WHO: 'as a minimum, in the care of all patients'; CDC: 'used for all patient care')
The specific PPE worn varies by task and expected exposure (risk assessment)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson distinguishes the always-on baseline (every patient, every time) from the task-based choice of which gear within that baseline — the standard CDC/WHO framing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'one needle, one syringe, only one time' is a CDC or WHO slogan
positions: CDC's One & Only Campaign uses the phrase 'One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time'
WHO injection-safety materials promote the same single-use standard worldwide
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson attributes the slogan to the CDC's One & Only Campaign (verified on the CDC page) and presents the single-use standard as the shared international norm.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-4 generated draft contained no factual clinical claims — it was generic boilerplate ('Standard Precautions is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations') with no definition, components, or evidence, so nothing in it survived the rewrite.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generic draft with a source-verified lesson: working definition attributed to CDC and WHO, components verified against both sources, safe-injection slogan verified against the CDC One & Only Campaign page, and all clinical claims cut unless supported by a source record.
